blocks.text: A patient with years of acid reflux has an endoscopic biopsy reporting that the lower oesophageal lining has changed from a stratified squamous to a columnar epithelium. To understand why that change matters, you must first be able to read an epithelium by cell shape, number of layers and the junctions that make the sheet a barrier.

blocks.markdown: Epithelia line surfaces, cavities and ducts and form glands. They sit on a **basement membrane** (basal lamina plus reticular lamina), are avascular, and are **polarised** with distinct apical and basal surfaces. Classification asks two questions: what is the **shape** of the surface cells, and how many **layers** are there?

blocks.title: Core classification terms
blocks.text: Shapes: squamous (flat), cuboidal (about as tall as wide) and columnar (taller than wide). Layers: simple (one layer), stratified (two or more layers), pseudostratified (a single layer in which every cell touches the basement membrane but nuclei lie at different heights) and urothelium or transitional epithelium (a stratified epithelium whose cells change shape as the organ stretches). Stratified epithelia are named by their surface cells.

rows: Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, small ducts
Tall, often with microvilli or cilia
About 4-6 when relaxed, about 2-3 when stretched
Large dome-shaped (umbrella) cells that flatten on stretch
Distension with a tight, impermeable barrier
blocks.caption: Epithelial types, locations and function (layer counts in urothelium are approximate and vary with distension)

blocks.title: Identifying an epithelium from a description
blocks.prompt: A slide shows a single layer of very flat cells with flat nuclei lining a gas-exchange space. Which epithelium is this?

steps.text: Combine: simple squamous epithelium, as in the alveoli.

blocks.title: Matching structure to function
blocks.prompt: A lining faces repeated abrasion from a passing food bolus and does not need rapid diffusion. Which epithelium suits it?

steps.text: Abrasion requires multiple layers so that surface cells can be shed while deeper cells remain.
Flat surface cells resist friction, so stratified squamous.
A moist surface means non-keratinised, as in the oesophagus.

blocks.markdown: **Why thin helps exchange.** Time for diffusion across a distance $x$ scales as $t \propto x^2$, so halving the thickness reduces diffusion time fourfold. **Why tall cells help absorption.** Microvilli increase the apical surface area of absorptive cells, giving the brush border of the small intestine; a cylinder of diameter $d$ and length $L$ has side area about $\pi d L$.

blocks.title: Junctions and their diseases
blocks.text: Tight junctions (claudins, occludin) seal neighbouring cells near the apex, limiting paracellular passage and maintaining polarity. Desmosomes (cadherins such as desmoglein linked to keratin intermediate filaments) are spot welds between cells that resist shear; autoantibodies to desmoglein cause pemphigus vulgaris, with epidermal cells separating from one another. Hemidesmosomes (integrins and BP180 linked to keratin) anchor the basal cell surface to the basement membrane; autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins cause bullous pemphigoid, with the whole epidermis lifting off its basement membrane.

items: One layer of flat cells: simple squamous; one layer of tall cells: simple columnar; one layer of cubes: simple cuboidal.
Nuclei at different heights but all cells touch the basement membrane: pseudostratified.
Many layers with flat surface cells: stratified squamous; epithelium that flattens and loses layers on stretch: urothelium.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not classify by nuclear position alone: in pseudostratified epithelium every cell reaches the basement membrane. Keep urothelium distinct from stratified squamous: its surface cells are large and dome-shaped, not flat, when relaxed.

points: Epithelia are classified by surface cell shape and layer number, and each type suits a function: exchange, absorption or secretion, or protection.
Urothelium has about 4-6 layers when relaxed and about 2-3 when stretched, as its dome cells flatten.
Tight junctions seal, desmosomes bind cells together, and hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basement membrane.

questions.stem: Thyroid follicles are lined by a single layer of cells about as tall as they are wide. What is the epithelium?

distractorRationale.c: Pseudostratified cells are tall with nuclei at varying heights.

questions.explanation: One layer of cube-shaped cells is simple cuboidal epithelium, typical of thyroid follicles, kidney tubules and small ducts.

questions.stem: A biopsy of a main bronchus shows tall cells with cilia and goblet cells, nuclei at several heights, and every cell touching the basement membrane. How is this epithelium classified?

distractorRationale.b: Stratified epithelium has cells that do not reach the basement membrane.
distractorRationale.c: Simple columnar has nuclei at a similar level.

questions.explanation: All cells contact the basement membrane, so it is a single layer functionally; the varying nuclear heights make it look layered. This arrangement with cilia and goblet cells supports mucociliary clearance.

questions.stem: A section of an empty bladder shows several cell layers with large dome-shaped surface cells; in a distended bladder the same epithelium shows fewer, flattened layers. Which epithelium is this?

distractorRationale.b: Stratified squamous surface cells are flat even when relaxed.
distractorRationale.c: Cuboidal epithelium is a single layer.
distractorRationale.d: Pseudostratified epithelium is a single layer.

questions.explanation: Urothelium accommodates distension by flattening its dome-shaped surface cells and thinning to roughly two to three layers, while maintaining an impermeable barrier. A stratified squamous epithelium does not change shape in this way.

questions.stem: Describe the structure and function of tight junctions, desmosomes and hemidesmosomes.
markingGuide: Tight junctions seal adjacent cells at the apex, limit paracellular passage and maintain polarity.
Desmosomes are cell-to-cell spot junctions linked to keratin filaments that resist shear.
Hemidesmosomes anchor the basal surface to the basement membrane (cell to matrix).
Distinguishes desmosomes (cell to cell) from hemidesmosomes (cell to matrix).
questions.explanation: A good answer separates the three junctions by location and function: seal, rivet between cells, and anchor to matrix.

questions.stem: The gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing water. Which epithelium is best suited to this task and why?

options.text: Simple columnar epithelium, because tall cells with microvilli carry out absorption
Stratified squamous epithelium, because multiple layers resist abrasion
Simple squamous epithelium, because flat cells give rapid gas exchange
Urothelium, because it stretches to hold urine

questions.correctOptionText: Simple columnar epithelium, because tall cells with microvilli carry out absorption

distractorRationale.b: Abrasion is not the main demand.
distractorRationale.c: Gas exchange is not the function.
distractorRationale.d: Stretch is not the problem solved here.

questions.explanation: Absorption requires cells tall enough to hold transport machinery and an apical surface expanded by microvilli, which suits simple columnar epithelium.

questions.stem: Diffusion time across a barrier scales with the square of its thickness. A type I alveolar epithelial cell is about 0.2 micrometres thick, while a simple columnar absorptive cell is about 20 micrometres tall. By what factor is diffusion across the columnar cell slower, all else equal? Give a dimensionless factor.
questions.explanation: Because diffusion time is proportional to thickness squared, the factor is (20 / 0.2)^2 = 100^2 = 10000. This is why gas-exchange surfaces are simple squamous and as thin as possible, whereas tall columnar cells suit absorption and secretion, not rapid diffusion.

questions.stem: An absorptive cell has 3000 cylindrical microvilli, each 1.0 micrometre long and 0.1 micrometre in diameter. Ignoring the tips, calculate the added surface area from their sides in square micrometres (use pi = 3.14).
questions.explanation: Side area of one microvillus is pi x d x L = 3.14 x 0.1 x 1.0 = 0.314 square micrometres. Times 3000 gives about 942 square micrometres, showing how a brush border enlarges absorptive surface.

questions.stem: A patient has blisters in which skin cells separate from each other; serum contains autoantibodies to desmoglein. Which junction is targeted?

distractorRationale.b: Hemidesmosome failure lifts the whole epidermis from the basement membrane.
distractorRationale.c: Tight junction failure causes leak, not blistering.
distractorRationale.d: That would be the hemidesmosome-matrix pathway.

questions.explanation: Desmoglein is a desmosomal cadherin holding keratinocytes together, so antibodies against it cause intraepidermal separation (pemphigus vulgaris). Hemidesmosome targeting in bullous pemphigoid produces subepidermal blisters instead.

questions.stem: A toxin degrades the claudin proteins of intestinal epithelial cells while leaving desmosomes and hemidesmosomes intact. What is the most direct effect?

options.text: Increased paracellular leakage and loss of the apical-basal barrier
Cells detach from the basement membrane as sheets
Cells separate from one another under shear
Microvilli disappear from the apical surface

questions.correctOptionText: Increased paracellular leakage and loss of the apical-basal barrier

distractorRationale.d: Microvilli are actin structures not formed by claudins.

questions.explanation: Claudins are core proteins of tight junctions, which seal the paracellular space. Loss allows substances to pass between cells and polarity to be disrupted.

questions.stem: Explain why the alveolus, the palm epidermis and the bladder are each lined by a different epithelium, relating structure to the functional requirement at each site.
markingGuide: Alveolus: simple squamous, thin for rapid diffusion.
Palm epidermis: keratinised stratified squamous for abrasion and water-loss resistance.
Bladder: urothelium that flattens and thins on distension (about 4-6 layers relaxed, fewer when stretched) with an impermeable barrier.
Links each epithelium to a functional demand.
questions.explanation: The question tests matching requirement to structure: thin for exchange, thick and keratinised for abrasion, and stretchable for storage.
